Mechanism of anaerobic digestion of cattle manure enhanced by oxygen 
and hydrogen nano-bubble water
Linpei Han , Hengbing Zhou , Lei Li *, Wenjie Ye , Peng Xu , Yongli Liu , Bin Zhan , Xuya Peng
Key laboratory of the Three Gorges Reservoir Region's Eco-environments, Ministry of Education, Institute of Environment and Ecology, Chongqing University, Chongqing, 
400045, PR China
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Anaerobic digestion
Nano-bubble water
Methane production
Hydrolysis efficiency
Hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis pathway
A B S T R A C T
This study investigates the efficacy and mechanisms of hydrogen/oxygen nano-bubble water (H2/O2-NBW) in 
enhancing anaerobic digestion (AD) performance. Batch experiments demonstrated that H2-NBW and O2-NBW 
significantly increased methane yields by 4.21 % to 16.98 % and 3.37 % to 13.43 %, respectively, compared to 
the control group (p < 0.05). Partial least squares path modeling and random forest algorithms identified 100 % 
H2-NBW and 80 %O2-NBW as optimal dosages. Under these optimal dosage conditions, semi-continuous tests 
revealed that methane production rates increased by 4.9-fold for H2-NBW and 4.1-fold for O2-NBW at an organic 
loading rate of 4 g volatile solids (VS)/(L⋅d) compared to the control group, while maintaining a stable output of 
157.01–163.66 mL/gVS⋅d at 5 g VS/(L⋅d) when the control failed. Mechanistic investigations indicated that O2- 
NBW generates hydroxyl radicals that reduce cellulose crystallinity by 39.81 % and upregulate hydrolytic en­
zymes such as xylanase, cellulase, protease, and α-glucosidase, targeting the regulation of hydrolytic and 
acidogenic bacteria (Sedimentibacter). In contrast, H2-NBW activates hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis through 
the stimulation of dehydrogenase, acetokinase, and coenzyme F420, along with the enrichment of DMER64 and 
Methanobacterium. Microbial co-occurrence network analysis indicated that the addition of NBW significantly 
altered microbial interaction patterns. Functional predictions confirmed that H2/O2-NBW specifically strength­
ened the putative metabolic pathways of hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis and hydrolysis-acidogenesis. The 
synergistic mechanism of physical deconstruction and biological regulation of nanobubble water revealed in this 
study has opened a new pathway for the development of technologies aimed at enhancing AD performance.
1. Introduction
In 2023, China's rapidly expanding livestock sector produced 97.48 
million tons of meat, 35.63 million tons of poultry eggs, and 42.81 
million tons of dairy products [1]. This intensive farming practice gen­
erates approximately 3.8 billion tons of manure annually; however, less 
than 60 % of this waste undergoes proper treatment [2]. Consequently, 
over 1.5 billion tons of agricultural waste are released into the envi­
ronment untreated each year. Such crude disposal methods not only 
squander nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium resources but also pre­
cipitate cascading environmental risks, including heavy metal accumu­
lation, eutrophication of water bodies, and greenhouse gas emissions, 
which have become significant bottlenecks hindering the green transi­
tion in agriculture. Under China's “dual carbon” strategy, which aims to 
achieve carbon peak by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2060, anaerobic 
digestion (AD) technology—known for its synergistic benefits of organic 
matter degradation, energy recovery, and carbon emission reduc­
tion—has been recognized as a crucial solution for addressing the 
challenges of agricultural waste management [3]. However, the unique 
three-dimensional heterogeneous structure of lignocellulose, particu­
larly the encapsulation effect of lignin on cellulose and hemicellulose, 
results in inefficient hydrolysis, with actual methane yields often falling 
below 60 % of the theoretical maximum [4]. Existing process 
enhancement techniques, such as co-digestion [5], bioaugmentation 
[6], and the application of chemical additives [7], can improve degra­
dation efficiency to a certain extent. However, these methods are often 
subject to risks, including seasonal instability in substrate supply, high 
costs associated with microbial agents and chemical reagents, and po­
tential secondary pollution resulting from chemical agents. These fac­
tors significantly limit their engineering applications. Therefore, the

In recent years, micro-aeration technology has been extensively re­
ported to enhance lignocellulosic hydrolysis [8], while the introduction 
of hydrogen into anaerobic digesters is widely recognized for biogas 
upgrading [9]. However, the direct introduction of gases such as O2 and 
H2 in gaseous form into AD systems presents challenges, including low 
apparent solubility and short retention time. To mitigate spikes in dis­
solved oxygen or sudden increases in hydrogen partial pressure caused 
by rapid gas escape—which can inhibit the activity of strict anaerobic 
methanogens and syntrophic microorganisms—precise dosing of these 
gases is crucial. This requirement undoubtedly complicates engineering 
operations. In contrast, incorporating gases into the liquid phase 
through specialized methods to create nano-bubble water (NBW) has 
emerged as a promising alternative [10]. NBW is an aqueous system 
characterized by a high density of stable submicron-sized bubbles 
(typically <1 μm), featuring a high specific surface area, low buoyancy, 
and prolonged residence periods, which together facilitate highly effi­
cient gas-liquid synergistic interfaces [11,12]. As a liquid-phase addi­
tive, NBW is easy to handle and significantly enhances the apparent 
solubility and retention time of poorly soluble gases such as H2 and O2. 
Thus, NBW can serve as an efficient gas delivery and sustained-release 
platform, effectively targeting various bottlenecks in AD. For instance, 
oxygen nano-bubble water (O2-NBW) can establish a stable micro‑oxy­
gen environment, stimulate facultative hydrolytic bacteria, and promote 
the enzymatic breakdown of recalcitrant lignocellulose, thereby over­
coming the rate-limiting step of hydrolysis [10]. Meanwhile, hydrogen 
nano-bubble water (H2-NBW) is anticipated to provide a continuous and 
stable electron donor (H2) for hydrogenotrophic methanogens, thereby 
accelerating the CO2 reduction methanogenesis process and directly 
increasing methane yield [13]. Additionally, the collapse of nano­
bubbles may generate localized high energy and free radicals (e.g., ⋅OH), 
potentially disrupting the lignin-carbohydrate complex and further 
enhancing substrate bioavailability [10]. Therefore, the enhancing ef­
fect of NBW arises from the intrinsic synergy between its role as a 
functionalized gas carrier and its physico-chemical effects, which extend 
far beyond simple gas-water mixing, enabling precise regulation of mi­
crobial metabolic pathways and reaction processes in AD systems 
[14,15].
From an engineering application perspective, the integration of NBW 
technology into existing AD systems is highly feasible. A key advantage 
of this technology lies in its ability to replace conventional dilution 
water (e.g., tap water, recycled water) used for adjusting feedstock solid 
content in existing processes with functionalized NBW, without altering 
the system's original hydraulic loading or feedstock solid concentration, 
and without increasing overall water consumption. More importantly, 
nano-bubble generators have evolved into highly modular and 
commercially mature equipment [8], which can be seamlessly inte­
grated into existing dilution water pipelines for on-demand production 
and automated dosing. This significantly enhances the engineering 
practicality and marketability of this technology. However, despite 
numerous studies documenting the beneficial effects of NBW addition 
on AD performance [10,16,17], most existing research is confined to 
batch experiments. There is a notable lack of systematic understanding 
regarding the long-term effects of NBW addition on the mechanisms 
governing the entire four-stage AD process. This is particularly true 
concerning its regulation of functional microbial community structure, 
dynamics of key enzyme activities, and metabolic pathways. This gap 
significantly hinders further optimization of the process and the large- 
scale application of NBW enhancement technology.
This study systematically investigates the enhancement mechanism 
of H2/O2-NBW on the AD process of cattle manure, addressing the 
identified scientific bottlenecks. Batch experiments with varying dos­
ages were designed to determine the optimal dosing ratios for H2-NBW 
and O2-NBW. Subsequently, long-term continuous experiments were 
conducted to elucidate the regulatory patterns of NBW on enzyme ac­
tivities related to hydrolysis and methanogenesis. Finally, an integrated 
microbial analysis was performed to clarify the reconfiguration mech­
anisms of the functional microbial community structure and metabolic 
pathways. By coupling enzymatic activity dynamics with microbial 
succession analysis, this study elucidates the long-term enhancement 
mechanisms,

and 
engineering-oriented optimization strategies for the valorization of 
agricultural waste.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Inoculum and substrate
The inoculum sludge utilized in this experiment was sourced from 
the anaerobic digester of the Tangjiatuo Wastewater Treatment Plant in 
Chongqing, China. After retrieval, the sludge was allowed to settle for 
three days to eliminate large inorganic particles, followed by centrifu­
gation to concentrate its total solids (TS) from 3 % to 8 %. The 
concentrated sludge was subsequently placed in a continuous stirred 
tank reactor with an effective volume of 15 L for acclimatization. 
Initially, no feeding was conducted to deplete the background organic 
matter present in the inoculum. Once the daily gas production fell below 
1 L, cattle manure was introduced as the substrate. Acclimatization 
occurred at an organic loading rate (OLR) of 3 g VS/L⋅d and a hydraulic 
retention time (HRT) of 30 days until the daily gas production fluctuated 
by no more than 10 % over a consecutive week, indicating the successful 
completion of sludge acclimatization [18]. Following this, continuous 
feeding was maintained under the original acclimatization conditions to 
sustain microbial activity for subsequent experiments. The cattle 
manure was collected from a small dairy farm in Chongqing and stored 
in a refrigerator at 4 ◦C for future use. The physicochemical properties of 
the acclimated inoculum sludge and substrate are presented in Table S1.
2.2. Nano-bubble water
In this study, O2-NBW and H2-NBW were produced using a nano- 
bubble water generator (Model RWP180, Ruke Environmental Protec­
tion Equipment Co., Ltd., Jiangsu, China) through the gas-water circu­
lation method [19]. Oxygen gas (purity ≥99.995 %) was obtained from 
Tianjin Anxing Industrial Gas Sales Co., Ltd. (China), while hydrogen gas 
(purity ≥99.995 %) was generated using a hydrogen generator. A total 
of 7.5 L of deionized water was circulated at a flow rate of 2.5 L/min, 
with the gas intake rate and pressure of the nano-bubble generator 
maintained at 0.07 L/min and 0.24 MPa, respectively. Continuous 
infusion of oxygen or hydrogen was conducted for 20 min to produce O2- 
NBW and H2-NBW [16,20]. The resulting NBW exhibited the following 
properties: average bubble sizes of 183.54 ± 24.32 nm and 214.39 ±
35.21 nm, bubble concentrations of 2.30 × 107 bubbles/mL and 2.40 ×
107 bubbles/mL, and zeta potentials of −31.65 ± 2.98 mV and −23.90 
± 1.32 mV for O2-NBW and H2-NBW, respectively. These key properties 
align with those reported in the literature [16,21,22], thereby con­
firming the robustness of our methodology and the validity of comparing 
our results with existing research. Additionally, the dissolved oxygen 
content of O2-NBW and the dissolved hydrogen concentration of H2- 
NBW were measured at 37.30 mg/L and 1360 ppb, respectively.
2.3. Batch experimental setup
Batch experiments were conducted using 500 mL serum bottles with 
a working volume of 400 mL. All reactors were established by adding 
cattle manure as the substrate and pre-acclimated inoculum sludge, 
which had been pre-incubated until gas production ceased, at a VS ratio 
(S/I) of 1.5. The TS concentration of the reactor contents was adjusted 
from 12.06 % to 8 % by adding dilution water, with a total of 111.30 mL 
added to each reactor. The control group utilized ultrapure water as the 
dilution medium, while the ten experimental groups received 20 %, 40 
%, 60 %, 80 %, and 100 % (volume ratio in dilution water) of either H2-

This experimental design aimed to investigate whether the use of 
functionalized NBW as dilution water can enhance the AD process 
compared to conventional dilution water. After a 5-min nitrogen purg­
ing, the serum bottles were sealed and incubated in a thermostatic water 
bath shaker at 37 ◦C with an agitation speed of 100 rpm. Samples from 
the reactors were collected on the 4th, 8th, 12th, 16th, 20th, and 25th 
days of the experiment to determine physicochemical parameters. The 
samples collected on the 25th day were additionally utilized to assess 
enzymatic activity. Furthermore, gas samples were collected daily using 
a syringe for gas composition analysis.
2.4. Gas sparging verification experiment
Following the identification of optimal dosage ratios for the two 
types of nanobubble water (100 %H2-NBW and 80 %O2-NBW) in the 
preceding experiments, a supplementary sparging control experiment 
was conducted. This experiment aimed to ascertain whether the 
enhanced reactor performance is attributable to the gases carried by the 
NBW or to the inherent synergy between its role as a functionalized gas 
carrier and its physicochemical effects. The reactor setup, S/I ratio, TS 
content of the mixture, and other experimental conditions were 
consistent with those described in Section 2.3. The configurations of the 
control group, 100 %H2-NBW, and 80 %O2-NBW groups also mirrored 
those in Section 2.3. Additionally, four sparging groups were estab­
lished, consisting of two groups for H2 and two groups for O2. Among 
these, two groups (H2 sparging at 22.81 mL and O2 sparging at 18.25 
mL) received aeration volumes equivalent to the total gas input during 
the generation of NBW, as calculated based on the preparation proced­
ure detailed in Section 2.2. The remaining two groups (H2 sparging at 
1.86 mL and O2 sparging at 2.55 mL) received aeration volumes that 
corresponded to the amount of gas entering the AD reactor via the NBW, 
which was back-calculated according to the measured dissolved gas 
concentrations in NBW. The detailed experimental design is illustrated 
in Fig. S1a. The aeration rate for the sparging groups was aligned with 
the gas injection rate of the nanobubble generator. Sparging was 
executed using a peristaltic pump (Rong Bai, BT100-2J), and all reaction 
conditions and gas sampling procedures adhered to those outlined in 
Section 2.3.
2.5. Semi-continuous reactor operation
To investigate the long-term effects of dilution water addition on 
reactor performance, ultrapure water, 100 %H2-NBW, and 80 %O2-NBW 
were selected as dilution waters for semi-continuous verification ex­
periments. A semi-continuous experiment was conducted using three 
acrylic continuous stirred-tank reactors, each with a working volume of 
15 L. Feeding and discharging occurred once daily. The acclimation of 
the inoculum and the preparation of the substrate are detailed in Section 
2.1. The reactor temperature was maintained at 37 ± 1 ◦C using a 
thermostatic control system. A top-mounted agitator operated at 100 
rpm for 4-h intervals, followed by 2-h pauses.
During the start-up phase (Phase I), the OLR was set at 3 g VS/(L⋅d), 
with an HRT of 30 days. The total mass of the feed was calculated based 
on the reactor's effective volume, OLR, and substrate characteristics. 
Subsequently, the digesters were fed after diluting the substrate with 
water to achieve a TS content of 10 %. Gas production from each reactor 
was measured daily to monitor operational status, while liquid samples 
were collected every two days to assess various physicochemical pa­
rameters. The transition between reactor phases and the increase in OLR 
adhered to performance-based criteria reported in the literature 
[23,24], where a pseudo-steady state was considered achieved if the 
daily biogas production fluctuation remained within 10 % for seven 
consecutive days. Upon meeting this criterion and ensuring that the 
reactor had operated for more than one HRT, the OLR was increased to 4 
g VS/(L⋅d) (Phase II). After maintaining stable operation for no less than 
one HRT at an OLR of 4 g VS/(L⋅d), the OLR was further elevated to 5 g 
VS/(L⋅d) (Phase III). Throughout each phase, dilution water was intro­
duced into the reactor alongside the substrate during the daily feeding 
operations for the entire experimental period. Microbial samples were 
collected at the conclusion of Phase I, Phase II, and Phase III, and stored 
at −80 ◦C in an ultra-low temperature refrigerator for subsequent mi­
crobial community analysis.
2.6. Analytical methods
The methods employed to monitor methane content and the con­
centrations of VFAs — including acetate, propionate, butyrate, iso­
butyrate, valerate, and isovalerate — along with pH, total alkalinity 
(ALK), partial alkalinity (PA), TS, VS, chemical oxygen demand (COD), 
ORP, ZETA potential, total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) concentration, 
soluble polysaccharides (PS), and soluble proteins (PN) were based on 
procedures described in previous studies [25,26]. The cellulose content 
in cattle manure was determined using the Van Soest method. The ac­
tivities of xylanase, acetate kinase, protease, coenzyme F420, α-glucosi­
dase, cellulase, and dehydrogenase were assessed according to 
methodologies outlined in prior researches [27,28]. The crystallinity 
index of cellulose in the samples, both before and after the AD experi­
ment, was evaluated based on the technique described by Wang et al. 
[29] The diluted water from the three experimental groups (i.e., the 
control group, 80 %O2-NBW group, and 100 %H2-NBW group) was 
analyzed for hydroxyl radicals present in NBW using an EMXmicro-9.5/ 
12/P/L type instrument for electron paramagnetic resonance spectros­
copy prior to being added to the reactor [30]. The concentrations of 
dissolved hydrogen in H2-NBW and dissolved oxygen in O2-NBW were 
measured directly using a portable dissolved hydrogen meter (Kedida, 
CT-8023 L) and a portable dissolved oxygen meter (Leici, JPBJ-608), 
respectively.

2.8. Microbial community structure analysis
Genomic DNA extraction was performed using the FastDNA®SPIN 
Kit for Soil (MP Biomedicals). The variable regions of the 16S rRNA 
genes were amplified via PCR employing modified universal primers 
338FmodF (GTGYCAGCMGCCGCGGTAA) and 806RmodR (GGAC­

an Illumina MiSeq platform (Majorbio). Bioinformatics processing 
encompassed raw data quality control, contig assembly, reference-based 
taxonomy annotation, α-diversity assessment, and community structure 
analysis, in accordance with established bioinformatics protocols from 
previous studies [25,31].
2.9. Statistical analyses
A one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted to test the 
differences in physicochemical indices among the groups. Descriptive

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Effect of nano-bubble water types and dose on reactor performance
3.1.1. Biogas production performance and kinetics
As illustrated in Fig. 1, the incorporation of H2-NBW and O2-NBW 
demonstrates differentiated enhancing effects on biogas production 
performance during the AD of cattle manure. In the H2-NBW system, the 
cumulative methane yield (CMY) of each experimental group showed a 
significant positive correlation with the addition ratio of H2-NBW in 
dilution water (correlation coefficient r = 0.756, p < 0.001, Fig. 1c). At a 
100 % dosage, the peak daily methane production increased by 9.48 % 
compared to the control group (Fig. 1a), and the CMY reached 286.13 
mL/g VS, representing a 16.98 % increase over the control group 
(Fig. 1b). This observation aligns with previous studies indicating that 
H2-NBW can gradually release H2 [32], thereby providing a substrate for 
methanogenesis. Notably, the dissolved hydrogen concentration in H2- 
NBW was measured at 1360 ppb. Even with the 100 %H2-NBW dosage, 
the total amount of hydrogen introduced into the reaction system 
alongside 111.30 mL of dilution water, was only 1.70 mL (under 
standard conditions). According to the stoichiometry of hydro­
genotrophic methanogenesis (4H2 + CO2 → CH4 + 2H2O), this quantity 
of hydrogen could theoretically yield only 0.425 mL of CH4. This amount 
is significantly lower than the methane production increments (474.74 
mL) observed in the 100 %H2-NBW group compared to the control 
group, indicating that the contribution rate of H2 as a substrate to the gas 
production increment is less than 0.1 %. This clearly suggests that the 
enhancement in methane production primarily arises from the unique 
properties of the nanobubble carrier itself, rather than its role in intro­
ducing a reactive substrate. The results from the sparging experiments 
further substantiate this inference (Fig. S1b). The CMY in the high and 
low-dosage groups increased by 4.61 % and 2.69 %, respectively, 
compared to the control group. The gas input volume in the low-dosage 
group was consistent with that of the 100 %H2-NBW group; however, 
the differences in gas delivery methods resulted in significant variations 
in gas production increments. This indicates that nanobubbles do not 
merely serve as gas ‘transport vehicles’; rather, they likely enhance the 
activity of methanogenic archaea more effectively through mechanisms 
such as stabilizing micro-interfaces, improving mass transfer, or directly 
interacting with microorganisms. Although the high-dosage group 
received a greater volume of gas input, it exhibited a pronounced lag 
period in gas production during the initial reaction phase. This obser­
vation demonstrates that H2 input via sparging is highly susceptible to 
inducing a high hydrogen partial pressure, which inhibits gas produc­
tion, thereby underscoring the advantages of nanobubble water- 
mediated gas delivery. Notably, even if the gas volumes from the high 
and low-dosage groups were entirely utilized for methane production, 
the theoretically calculated methane increments would only be 5.70 mL 
and 0.465 mL, respectively, still representing less than 5 % of the total 
gas production increase in each group. This illustrates that whether H2 is 
introduced via nanobubble water or sparging, the contribution rate of 
H2 as a substrate to the gas production increment remains extremely 
low.

reaching 277.45 mL/g VS, which was 13.43 % and 10.65 % higher than 
that of the control group (244.59 mL/g VS) and the 100 %H2-NBW

that the appropriate addition of O2-NBW can significantly enhance 
methane yield during the AD of cattle manure. Furthermore, the results 
from the oxygen sparging experiments further validate the substantial 
advantage of using NBW as a gas carrier over direct sparging. As illus­

amount introduced via the 80 %O2-NBW) was supplied to the reactor 
through sparging, the O2 sparging group exhibited no stimulatory effect 
on methanogenesis, with the CMY decreasing by 0.43 % compared to the 
control group. In contrast, the CMY in the O2 sparging group was only 
8.91 % of that in the control group when the amount of O2 was equal to 
the total gas volume used in the NBW preparation process. This indicates 
that, for both hydrogen and oxygen, sparging an equivalent volume of 
gas resulted in a lesser enhancement of methane production compared 
to the NBW groups. Moreover, when introduced at volumes matching 
the total gas used in NBW preparation, sparging caused varying degrees 
of inhibition in either methane production or methane production ki­
netics. In conclusion, utilizing NBW as a gas carrier and leveraging its 
gas-liquid synergistic interface leads to improved reactor performance 
compared to sparging, with the primary contribution arising from the 
holistic effect of NBW rather than the introduced gases serving as direct 
substrates for methane production.
The modified Gompertz model was employed to fit the biogas pro­
duction kinetics across various AD systems, achieving a coefficient of 
determination (R2) of ≥0.998. As illustrated in Fig. 1b, the Rmax of the 
100 %H2-NBW group was measured at 21.06 mL/g VS, reflecting a 
significant increase of 8.11 % compared to the control, which recorded 
19.48 mL/g VS (p < 0.05). Notably, the λ exhibited a significant 
decreasing trend from 1.69 to 1.55 days (p < 0.05) with the increasing 
proportion of H2-NBW, suggesting that the introduction of H2 acceler­
ated the microbial community's adaptation to the system [35]. The ki­
netic response of the O2-NBW group exhibited a nonlinear characteristic, 
as shown in Fig. 1e. The Rmax for the 80 %O2-NBW group significantly 
increased by 10.52 %, reaching 21.53 mL/g VS compared to the control 
group (19.48 mL/g VS, p < 0.05). However, when the proportion of O2- 
NBW increased to 100 %, Rmax decreased to 19.69 mL/g VS, showing no 
significant difference from the control (p > 0.05). This further indicates 
that a high proportion of O2-NBW may diminish its potential to enhance 
methane production, potentially due to an excessively high redox po­
tential. The results preliminarily indicate that the enhancing effect of 
NBW is closely associated with the type and dosage of the gas it carries; 
thus, the optimal proportions of H2-NBW and O2-NBW should be 
maintained at 100 % and 80 %, respectively, to achieve maximum 
positive stimulation.
3.1.2. Characteristics of substrate degradation and enzyme activity
Differences in substrate degradation characteristics reflect the dif­
ferential regulation by NBW during the hydrolysis and acidogenesis 
phases. Fig. 2a and b illustrate the variation patterns of soluble PN and 
PS across the experimental groups, respectively. Soluble PN and PS are 
hydrolyzed from complex organic materials in the substrate during the 
initial phase of AD. A comparison of concentrations between experi­
mental groups on days 4 and 8 revealed that the soluble PS and PN 
concentrations in the H2-NBW and O2-NBW groups were generally 
higher than those in the control group. Specifically, the 100 %H2-NBW 
and 80 %O2-NBW groups exhibited significant increases in soluble PS 
and PN concentrations of 9.66 %–9.93 % and 17.98 %–27.73 % on day 4 
(p < 0.05), and 12.44 %–15.02 % and 11.28 %–15.85 % on day 8 (p <
0.05), respectively. These results demonstrate that both types of NBW 
enhance substrate hydrolysis to varying degrees. Notably, the soluble PN 
and PS contents in all experimental groups exhibited an initial increase 
followed by a decrease over time. This trend significantly deviates from 
the typical monotonically decreasing pattern of soluble organic matter 
reported in previous studies [11]. This anomaly may arise from the 
transient solubilization of particulate organic matter, the release of 
microbial cell lysis products, or analytical interference caused by 
colloidal substances. The underlying mechanisms warrant further 
investigation. Fig. 2c illustrates the differences in removal efficiencies of 
cellulose, TS, and VS across the experimental groups. The results indi­
cate that the removal efficiencies of cellulose, TS, and VS in the 100 %

3.1.3. Path modeling and non-linear interrelations
This study elucidates the differential regulatory mechanisms of the 
AD process influenced by H2/O2-NBW, utilizing PLS-PM in conjunction 
with RFA (Fig. 3). The model's goodness-of-fit (GoF > 0.72) and the 
explanatory power of the latent variables (R2 > 0.7) confirm the reli­
ability of the results. In the 100 %H2-NBW group, model analysis 
revealed that the enhancement of key enzyme activities, such as coen­
zyme F420 and dehydrogenase, constitutes the primary pathway driving 
methane production. Specifically, the PLS-PM demonstrated a signifi­
cant path coefficient of 0.470 (p < 0.05) from enzyme activity to 
methane production (Fig. 3a and c). Additionally, RFA model analysis 
indicated contributions of 6.11 % for coenzyme F420 (p < 0.001) and 
6.04 % for dehydrogenase (p < 0.01) (Fig. 3e). These findings suggest 
that H2-NBW enhances efficiency primarily by significantly increasing 
enzymatic activity in methanogenic terminal metabolism, particularly 
in hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis dependent on coenzyme F420.
In stark contrast, the impact pathway of the 80 %O2-NBW group was 
primarily characterized by an enhancement in the conversion of front- 
end substrate hydrolysis. The PLS-PM indicated that the physicochem­
ical properties positively influenced the accumulation of VFAs, with a 
path coefficient of 0.891 (p < 0.001). This accumulation subsequently 
led to a significant increase in methane production, as evidenced by a 
path coefficient of 1.095 for the conversion from VFAs to methane (p <
0.05) (Fig. 3b). Furthermore, the RFA model substantiated the critical 
contributions of hydrolytic enzymes, revealing that cellulase contrib­
uted 7.68 %, xylanase 7.61 %, and protease 7.19 % to the process (p <
0.01). These findings suggest that O2-NBW enhances methane produc­
tion primarily by improving hydrolytic enzyme activity, thereby opti­
mizing substrate deconstruction and acidogenesis efficiency. In 
summary, the model analyses reaffirm a fundamental divergence in the 
enhancement mechanisms between the two types of NBW: H2-NBW 
primarily targets the direct optimization of terminal methanogenesis, 
whereas O2-NBW focuses on augmenting front-end hydrolysis and 
acidogenesis efficiency. Based on the physicochemical and biochemical 
indicators, it is evident that 100 %H2-NBW and 80 %O2-NBW represent 
the optimal addition dosages.

widely recognized as a marker for methanogenesis [35]. The prediction 
abundance of methyl-CoM reductase (MCR) in the H2-NBW group 
increased by 44.34 % and 38.10 % compared to the control and O2-NBW 
groups, respectively. This suggests that H2-NBW may enrich hydro­
genotrophic methanogens harboring the MCR gene (e.g., Meth­
anobacterium) and enhance the genetic capacity for methanogenesis. 
Such changes may improve the terminal methanogenic stage of AD by 
activating hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis. Conversely, the predic­
tion abundance of MCR in the O2-NBW group showed no significant 
change compared to the control group, further confirming that the 
micro-oxic environment induced by O2-NBW may suppress the func­
tional potential of methanogens, potentially due to hydroxyl radical- 
mediated DNA damage.
In summary, H2/O2-NBW optimizes AD processes through distinct 
metabolic regulation strategies. The addition of H2-NBW appears to 
activate the genetic encoding potential of key genes involved in 
hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis, while the introduction of O2-NBW 
emphasizes the enhancement of the hydrolysis and acidogenesis stages. 
Its micro-oxic properties may potentially suppress the functional ca­
pacity of methanogens. It is important to acknowledge that functional 
predictions are inherently less accurate than quantitative gene expres­
sion analyses. Therefore, future studies should employ hydrogen isotope 
tracing techniques to directly quantify H2 conversion pathways and 
conduct systematic hydrogen balance accounting. Additionally, meta­
transcriptomic or targeted gene quantification approaches should be 
utilized to analyze the expression levels of key functional genes, such as 
mcrA, fwd, and hyaB. This integrated methodology will establish

4. Conclusion
This study elucidates the potential and mechanisms underlying the 
targeted enhancement of AD using H2/O2-NBW. Batch experiment re­
sults demonstrated that H2-NBW primarily activated dehydrogenase, 
coenzyme F420, and acetokinase, leading to an enhancement in methane 
yield of 4.21 %–16.98 % compared to the control group. In contrast, O2- 
NBW facilitated a positive feedback loop of substrate supply and meta­
bolic conversion through hydroxyl radical-mediated deconstruction of 
cellulose crystallinity, which decreased by 39.81 %, and enhanced hy­
drolytic enzyme activity, resulting in methane yield and cellulose 
removal efficiency increases of 3.37 %–13.43 % and 2.75 %–132.13 %, 
respectively, compared to the control group. PLS-PM and RFA results 
indicated that the primary influencing factors for methane production in 
the H2-NBW and O2-NBW groups were coenzyme F420 and cellulase, 
respectively. Furthermore, 100 %H2-NBW and 80 %O2-NBW were 
identified as optimal additive dosages. Semi-continuous experiments 
revealed that the H2/O2-NBW groups maintained a methane yield of 
157.01–163.66 mL/gVS⋅d at a high OLR of 5 gVS/(L⋅d). The microbial 
co-occurrence network analysis indicated that the addition of NBW 
significantly altered microbial interaction patterns. Among them, the 
H2-NBW group enriched functional bacteria related to hydrogenotrophic 
methanogenesis and acetogenesis, including DMER64 and Meth­
anobacterium, while O2-NBW targeted the regulation of Sedimentibacter, 
which belong to hydrolytic and acidogenic bacteria. Functional pre­
dictions indicated that H2/O2-NBW enhanced key metabolic pathways 
related to hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis and hydrolysis/acido­
genesis, respectively. Future research should focus on comparing the 
effects of direct gas addition with those of NBW, as well as quantitatively 
analyzing the direct contribution of dissolved hydrogen in H2-NBW to 
methane production through the CO2 reduction pathway. Such in­
vestigations will significantly enhance our understanding of the poten­
tial mechanisms underlying the effects of nanobubble water.
